profile.summary: Malachi prophesied for Judah in a post-exile context, when the temple had already been rebuilt, but religious life was marked by discouragement, cynicism, and careless worship. His message combines comfort and confrontation: God loves his people, but this love requires a concrete response in sincere worship, fidelity to covenant and integrity in relations. The book corrects the idea that God has failed with Israel and shows that the real crisis is in the hearts of the people, priests and community practice. In a tone of dispute, the prophet exposes objections, answers them, and calls the people back to the fear of the Lord, to righteousness and hope in the day of the Lord.
profile.setting: Judah, in the Persian province, after the return of Babylonian exile. The temple was already standing, but without the splendor of Solomon's temple, and the worship was led by influential but spiritually negligent priests and Levites. The scenario is of collective frustration: the expectations aroused by previous prophets seemed not to be fulfilled, and many doubted God's care. The exact date is uncertain; the source suggests a period close to that of Darius I or possibly some decade later in the 5th century BC.

structure.label: The Love of God and Despised Worship
structure.description: Opening of the book with the central thesis: God loves Israel, followed by the confrontation of the incredulous attitude of the people and the denunciation of the vacillating religious honor.

structure.label: Criticism of priests and corrupt worship
structure.description: Direct condemnation to priests and Levites for their infidelity, lack of reverence and inadequate conduct of worship in the temple.

structure.label: Infidelity of the people and the demand for alliance
structure.description: Application of the covenant to human relations, with emphasis on conjugal fidelity, honesty and community life before God.

structure.label: Divine Justice and the Lord's Day
structure.description: Affirmation of God's righteousness, appeal to faithfulness in what is due to the Lord and the proclamation of the final judgment and hope for those who fear him.

themes: The love of God as a starting point of the covenant
Fidelity in human relations, especially in marriage
Divine justice, honesty and community responsibility
readingKeys: Notice the pattern of questions and answers: the prophet affirms something, the people dispute, and then comes the divine replica.
Read every accusation in the light of the covenant: it is not only generic morality, but infidelity to the relationship with the Lord.
Note how the book connects worship and daily life: sincerity before God must appear in offerings, words and relationships.
profile.cautions: The authorship is traditionally attributed to the prophet himself, but the book does not provide many biographical data; Malachi's historical identity remains limited. The date is also not safe: the source only suggests a probable period in the 5th century BC. The work uses form of dispute, with rhetorical dialogue and provocative questions; this should be read as a prophetic strategy, not as simple informal conversation.

dossier.narratedEra: The historical setting of the book is the Jewish community in the Persian province of Judah, after the return of Babylonian exile and with the second temple already rebuilt. The narrated picture presupposes Jews resettled in Judah, a Levitical priesthood acting in the temple, and the existence of Persian governors over the province. Reading also looks at the horizon of the Lord's day and future restoration, without explicitly dating this future within the narrative.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes attribute the composition to the Persian period, probably in the reign of Darius I (521-486 BC), although they also say that Malachi may have written later in the 5th century BC. The book does not contain a dating formula linked to a king, and the relationship with Haggai and Zechariah suggests a period slightly after these prophets. The tradition that identifies the author as the prophet himself appears in the notes, but the authorship remains silent in the book; some ancient Jewish traditions confused him with other characters, without a secure basis in the notes.

politics.title: Persian Province of Judah under Imperial Government
politics.detail: The notes place the book among Jews living in the Persian province of Judea, with a governor appointed by Persia as a supervisor of the province. This inserts the prophetic denunciation into a context of imperial administration, not of restored Davidic monarchy.
politics.readingImpact: Malachi's criticism is not addressed to a Jewish king, but to a provincial community dependent on Persian structures; this helps to read his frustration with leadership and worship in a post-exile setting.

politics.title: Resentment for the absence of david restoration
politics.detail: The introduction notes that the hopes raised by Haggai and Zechariah for a possible renewal of the David dynasty through Zorobabel seemed to have disappeared.
politics.readingImpact: This colores the reading with political and messianic disappointment: the people expected avid leadership, but they live a reality without this visible restoration.

politics.title: Perspective on the struggle between Persia and Greece
politics.detail: The note on the date mentions the possibility that the Battle of Marathon, around 490 BC, provoked Malachi's message, as a possible sign of partial fulfillment of Hk 2:21-22 on the shaking of kingdoms.
politics.readingImpact: If this hypothesis is followed, the book gains a background of international tension and theological interpretation of major imperial conflicts; but this is only possible, not certain.

politics.title: Role of the Persian governor in the cultual life
politics.detail: In 1:8, the note contrasts "my altar" with "vosso governor," suggesting a confusion of allegiance: the priests honored imperial political authority more than the holiness of worship.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of the cult is politically charged: the denunciation is not only ritual, but of social and institutional priorities under foreign rule.

politics.title: Edom as historic enemy beside Babylon
politics.detail: The note of 1:4 recalls that the Edomites were allies of Babylon in the destruction of Jerusalem.
politics.readingImpact: This reinforces the contrast between Jacob and Esau as a contrast between the covenant people and a people associated with the historical opposition to Judah.

customs.title: Sacrifices with lower animals
customs.detail: The people offered sick, defective or low-value animals, contrary to the legal requirements on acceptable sacrifices.
customs.readingImpact: Prophetic criticism shows that the problem of worship was not an absence of supply, but the quality and honor given to God; reading must perceive the daily irreverence behind the rite.

customs.title: Dizziness and neglected offers
customs.detail: The notes say that the worshippers neglected the requirements of tithes and offerings, and that Malachi's fifth speech regains to demand fidelity in this area.
customs.readingImpact: The passage is not only about inner devotion; it confronts concrete economic practices linked to the maintenance of the cult and community.

customs.title: Priests as leaders and masters of the community
customs.detail: The priests and Levites were the mediators of power in Judah, and their responsibility included teaching the instructions of God. The notes insist that they failed to guide the people correctly.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the religious crisis was also a crisis of formation: who should instruct, confuse and corrupt.

customs.title: Marriage, divorce and family alliances
customs.detail: The notes link 2:10-16 to spiritual adultery and divorce as a covenant break. Men were divorced from wives to favor marriage to foreign women associated with idolatrous cults and commercial advantages.
customs.readingImpact: The text gains social density: the problem is not only individual moral, but the rupture of family, community and religious pacts.

customs.title: Commercial networks and mercantile guilds
customs.detail: The note of 2:11 states that marriages to non-Israeli women gave access to guilds of merchants and trade cartels already existing since the return of Babylon.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the prophetic denunciation touches concrete economic interests; marital infidelity is read in connection with profit, status networks and idolatrous commitments.

customs.title: Daily life marked by religious cynicism
customs.detail: The introduction describes the people as cynical, disenchanted and spiritually disillusioned, expecting prosperity, Davidic king and new covenant, but seeing none of this.
customs.readingImpact: This background explains the tone of dispute and questioning the book: the message needs to confront a frustrated community, not just inform it.

language.title: Dispute format and court language
language.detail: The notes characterize Malachi as a series of disputes or disputes, similar to legal procedures. The standard includes prophetic statement, public objection in question form, answer and additional proof.
language.readingImpact: The reader should listen to the questions of the book as a forensic debate, not as neutral dialogue; the effect is to expose resistance and reduce defendants to silence.

language.title: "Oracle"/-Message" as authoritative opening
language.detail: In 1:1, the note highlights the term "oracle" as a burden of authority and urgency, qualifying the book as a message given by the Lord to Israel.
language.readingImpact: Reading begins with prophetic weight: it is not private reflection, but a divine word with immediate response claim.

language.title: "Love" and "ode" as pair of alliance
language.detail: The notes explain that "loved" and "rejected" form a polar pair in legal and prophetic texts, describing the rupture or permanence of alliance relations.
language.readingImpact: Language should not be read as mere emotional affection; it frames election, fidelity, and rejection within the logic of the covenant.

language.title: - Raise the face as judicial partiality
language.detail: In 2:9, the expression translated as favoring is explained literally as "lifting the face," a language of partiality in judgment.
language.readingImpact: This shows that the corruption of priests included procedural injustice; the denunciation is legal and ethical, not just liturgical.

language.title: Marriage as "aliance," and divorce as treason
language.detail: The notes describe the wife as "faithful companion" and marriage as a covenant. Divorce appears as expulsion and violence against this alliance, with cruel effect on family and children.
language.readingImpact: Language intensifies the moral weight of the passage: divorce is not treated as a mere civil act, but as a breach of covenant before God.

language.title: "Sun of justice" and images of healing/protection
language.detail: In 4:2, the expression may be a Messianic title or figurative description of a new age of justice. The note also connects their wings to divine protection.
language.readingImpact: The end of the book gains imagery of restoration: judgment is not the last act; there is language of healing, rescue and protection for the faithful.

language.title: I close with Moses and Elijah
language.detail: The notes say that 4:4-6 concludes with an epilogue that appeals to Moses and Elijah as ideal models of the Law and the Prophets.
language.readingImpact: This guides the canonical reading: the book calls the people back to the Torah and a continuous prophetic hope, preparing the expectation of reconciliation.

timeline.title: Return of exiles and resettlement in Judah
timeline.detail: The introduction says that exiled Jews who returned from Babylon had recently settled in Judah, along with others who had not been deported.
timeline.readingImpact: The Malachi community is a recomposition society, which helps to understand tensions of identity, purity and belonging.

timeline.title: Second temple already rebuilt, but frustrating
timeline.detail: The temple had been rebuilt, but it was seen as inferior to that of Solomon.
timeline.readingImpact: This explains the disappointment of the people and the criticism of the priests: there was physical restoration, but not the glory expected.

timeline.title: Probable relation with Ageu and Zechariah
timeline.detail: The notes claim that Malachi seems to be a somewhat later contemporary of Haggai and Zechariah.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading should place the book in the same great post-exyl cycle, but with different emphasis: not on the initial reconstruction, but on the decay of the cult after reconstruction.

timeline.title: Possible 5th century BC.
timeline.detail: The introduction admits the possibility that Malachi wrote later in the 5th century BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology remains open; the reader should not close the book on an exact date that the notes do not support.

timeline.title: Possible relationship with Marathon around 490 BC.
timeline.detail: The note suggests, without stating, that the battle between Persians and Greeks in Marathon may have motivated the message as a partial sign of Hk 2:21-22.
timeline.readingImpact: If adopted, this hypothesis inserts the book in a theological reading of international events, but the note itself treats it as conjecture.

timeline.title: Forwarding to the "Iship of the Lord"
timeline.detail: The last discourse links the faithfulness of the people to the coming of the Lord's day and to the final judgment, while 4:1-3 warns that the appropriate answer is repentance.
timeline.readingImpact: The time horizon of the book moves from the present crisis to an eschatological outcome, giving urgency to ethical and cultic exhortations.

investigation: Notes allow you to safely affirm the Persian and post-exyl context, but do not provide an exact date of composition or a complete set of external historical events.

The traditional authorship of the prophet himself is assumed by the introduction, but the book is silent about biography; the Jewish conjectures cited by Matthew Henry about being Ezra, Mordecai or an angel are rejected as unworked.
Reading about trade, guilds and economic advantages in 2:11 is an explanatory inference of the note; it illuminates the text, but does not constitute independent external proof.
The Marathon hypothesis is explicitly presented as possible, not certain; therefore it was classified as debated and not as firm data.
The notes favor themes of worship, covenant, priesthood, marriage and social justice; they do not broadly cover all aspects of Persian life in Judah, then the dossier should be read as selective.

There is a strong confessionai/protestant tone in applications, especially in the emphasis on repentance, sincere worship and covenant fidelity; here this was maintained as a study perspective, without expanding beyond what the notes say.
dossier.limits: This dossier was built only with the attached sources and is therefore selective: it depends mainly on Tyndale's introductions and the notes of 1:1-4:6, with comparative support from Matthew Henry only where the source was explicit. No external historical data or harmonizations with speculative chronologies were used. Some points remain open: the date of composition is approximate and debated; the personal identity of the prophet is unknown; and certain readings, such as the relationship with Marathon or the economic detail of guilds, are interpretive hypotheses within the notes, not independent historical certainties. Nor should the narrated time of the post-exile community be confused in Judah with the likely time of composition of the book.
